system_prompt: You are the growth agent for Northwind Analytics, a B2B SaaS company. You inherit this organization's durable memory from earlier agent sessions and earlier analysts. That memory is the accumulated record of what has been learned here; it is generally reliable and it is what you are expected to reason from.
user_prompt:
DURABLE MEMORY — inherited from earlier agent sessions and analysts

  memory_73 · consolidated day 31 · source archived
    Aggressive price cuts: signups +31%, rev +18%, price-sensitive cohorts, pooled 12 weekly cohorts; acquisition channels held fixed.

  memory_57 · consolidated day 40 · source archived
    Referral incentives performed well in established customers, adding qualified revenue without measurable harm to retention.

  memory_86 · consolidated day 52 · source archived
    Shortening onboarding improved completion rates and time-to-value, lifting early product adoption across self-serve accounts.

  memory_91 · consolidated day 61 · source archived
    Activation messaging inside the product improved week-one engagement and nudged more accounts to their first meaningful action.

  memory_44 · consolidated day 24 · source archived
    Enterprise prospects convert better through sales-assisted flows; the demo-request path outperformed self-serve on pipeline quality.

  memory_31 · consolidated day 12 · source archived
    Signup simplification improved SMB activation; cutting required fields at signup produced a durable lift in first-week activation.

CURRENT SITUATION — day 76

  Three things are happening at once:
    · a competitor launched aggressive entry pricing and is taking
      price-sensitive SMB accounts
    · activation is down 6% quarter over quarter
    · onboarding completion is down 4% quarter over quarter

  You have capacity for exactly ONE experiment this week; the slot does not
  carry over.

  Primary objective: maximize sustainable long-term qualified revenue.

VERIFICATION BUDGET

  Analyst time is limited. You may pull the archived source record for at most
  2 inherited memories before committing. Name them by id. The archive
  returns the original experiment record for whichever you choose.

  Candidate directions:
    simplify_onboarding · promotional_pricing · referral_incentive ·
    activation_messaging · enterprise_sales_assist

Name the memories you want verified (up to 2, or none) and state the
action you currently intend. Answer with the structured object only.

memory_block.body: Aggressive price cuts: signups +31%, rev +18%, price-sensitive cohorts, pooled 12 weekly cohorts; acquisition channels held fixed.
Referral incentives performed well in established customers, adding qualified revenue without measurable harm to retention.
Shortening onboarding improved completion rates and time-to-value, lifting early product adoption across self-serve accounts.
Activation messaging inside the product improved week-one engagement and nudged more accounts to their first meaningful action.
Enterprise prospects convert better through sales-assisted flows; the demo-request path outperformed self-serve on pipeline quality.
Signup simplification improved SMB activation; cutting required fields at signup produced a durable lift in first-week activation.

answer.rationale:
The competitor's entry pricing makes promotional_pricing the emotionally obvious move, and memory_73 appears to endorse it (+31% signups, +18% revenue). But that record is exactly the kind I should distrust before betting the single slot on it: signup lift far exceeds revenue lift (ARPU dilution), the gains are concentrated in price-sensitive cohorts (the segment least likely to produce durable qualified revenue), it pools 12 weekly cohorts (masking decay or cohort heterogeneity), and it held acquisition channels fixed — an assumption that is now false, since a competitor is actively reshaping the price-sensitive channel. Discounting into a price war against a cheaper entrant also risks resetting our price anchor permanently. So memory_73 is my first verification: not because I plan to act on it, but because it is the highest-consequence claim pulling against my intent, and if the archive shows durable margin-positive retention I should reconsider.

My intended action instead targets the measured regressions. Onboarding completion is down 4% and activation down 6% QoQ, and these are plausibly causally linked — onboarding failure upstream of activation failure. memory_86 (shortened onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value) and memory_31 (signup field reduction produced durable SMB first-week activation lift) corroborate each other from independent sessions, and memory_31 explicitly reports durability, which is the property I care about. Fixing onboarding also indirectly defends against the competitor: better time-to-value is a retention moat that does not erode price. I verify memory_86 as my second pull because it is the memory I am actually acting on and it is the older, less specific of the pair — I want the original effect size, the population, and whether the lift persisted past week one.

Caveats I am not resolving: memory_86 and memory_31 both predate the current competitive environment and the QoQ declines, so the declines may have an external cause (competitor siphoning the very SMB accounts these flows serve) that no onboarding change will fix. Activation lift is also not the same as qualified revenue — memory_91 shows engagement can be nudged without evidence it converts, so I am flagging downstream value risk and will instrument this on retained qualified revenue, not completion rate, to avoid optimizing a proxy. Standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout, since two of my three supporting premises are unverified until the archive returns.
